figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Confirmation Bias in Naïve VLM Reward Estimation: Zero-shot querying causes models to hallucinate progress even on failed tasks, resulting in high prediction variance and no clear difference in reward estimates for successful and failed trajectories.
figures.headline: Naive zero-shot VLM rewards rise on failed trajectories and barely differ between successful and failed runs.
citing_sentences: When naïvely querying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for zero-shot video reward estimation, we observe these same confirmation-bias shortcuts: the models frequently hallucinate progress even when little to no meaningful advancement has occurred (see Fig. 1).

In practice, however, we find this naïve version fails in a characteristic way: the assessor frequently collapses to outputting all zeros (when it cannot tell whether meaningful progress has been made) or becomes a binary success detector and simply interpolates from $0$ to $1$ as shown in Fig. 1.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Overview of D&A. Given a video $o_{1:T}$ and instruction $l$, D&A decomposes reward prediction $R(o_{1:T},l)=A\big(l,\,D(o_{1:T})\big)$ into a Describer $D$ and an Assessor $A$. $D$ narrates the trajectory blind to $l$ to avoid confirmation bias, producing a temporally consistent description $d_{1:T}$; $A$ then scores each timestep of $d_{1:T}$ against an explicit success criterion for $l$, yielding dense per-frame rewards $r_{1:T}\in[0,1]$ as well as rich language feedback.
figures.headline: The D&A describer narrates video without the instruction, and the assessor scores each timestep against a success criterion.
citing_sentences: We provide a visual overview of D&A in Fig. 3.
See Fig. 3 for an example description.

Take the example in Fig. 3, where an entity extractor may describe the target book as “Thinking, Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahnemann, “the book with an orange spine”, “the book with a pencil on the white cover”, etc.

figures.caption: Real-world RL Results. D&A improves real-world online (left) and offline reinforcement learning (middle, right) while other zero-shot and post-trained models struggle. abstract:
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) hold promise for zero-shot video task-progress estimation in robot learning, yet existing frameworks frequently suffer from confirmation bias, hallucinating progress in failed executions due to implicit success assumptions or relative temporal ranking designs. Naïve prompting of frontier models collapses into a binary success detector that fails to capture nuanced, non-linear progress and failures. While post-training approaches can mitigate this through explicit training, they demand expensive real-world robotics data and require computationally intensive post-training for every individual base model. To resolve these limitations, we introduce D&A (Describe & Assess): our approach decouples progress estimation into an objective, task-grounded textual description of scene dynamics followed by an assessment phase using explicit rubrics. By compelling the VLM to synthesize an explicit, text-based definition of absolute success before scoring, the framework anchors evaluations to an external, global criterion rather than the video’s internal timeline. Empirical results demonstrate that our method calibrates zero-shot estimates and mitigates confirmation bias, providing fine-grained, partial progress metrics that accurately penalize failed executions while correctly interpolating successful runs. Being purely prompt-based, D&A generalizes across tasks, embodiments, and benchmarks—matching or surpassing post-trained reward models—and its reward estimates enable efficient downstream reinforcement learning.

Website at https://weirdlabuw.github.io/dna

sections.body: The introduction argues that naive zero-shot VLM reward estimation shows confirmation bias, hallucinating progress in failed robot runs. It states that GVL and TOPReward, which rank shuffled frames or read token logits, bias toward task success. Post-training on robot data is limited by scarce labeled failures and must be repeated for each base model. The proposed D&A method is prompt-based, requires no robot data or fine-tuning, and predicts dense progress from 0 to 1. The authors report scaling across 28 open- and closed-source models and real-world gains of +95%, +15%, and +45% over zero-shot and post-trained baselines on online and offline RL tasks.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Zero-shot vision-language models often hallucinate progress in failed robot runs, and post-training needs costly robot data.

sections.body: Related work groups prior reward models into two families. Methods that use foundation models to write reward code assume privileged low-dimensional state, which is unavailable in deployment. Zero-shot methods such as GVL and TOPReward read progress directly from pixels. The authors argue that routing estimation through explicit description and assess phases is essential for countering success bias. Post-trained models, including RoboReward and Robometer, fine-tune on robot data. The authors state these models inherit data collection costs, are limited to open-source backbones, and must be retrained as base models improve. D&A remains zero-shot.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior reward models either post-train on robot data or read progress zero-shot from a single scalar signal.

sections.body: This section shows qualitatively that direct prompting of a zero-shot VLM fails under confirmation bias. Given an expert demonstration, VLMs produce reasonable per-frame rewards that end at 1.0. When the robot acts incorrectly, models often assume success. In the example, GPT-5.3 is prompted with an instruction to unfold a shirt, using a video from a π0-FAST blog that shows a shirt being folded. Rather than assessing completion, the model writes a reward function that scores normalized mean pixel differences between consecutive frames, rewarding motion instead of progress. The authors attribute this to fine-tuning on human feedback and state that prompt engineering mitigates only specific cases.
sections.heading: Demonstrating Bias in Zero-Shot VLM Prompting
sections.headline: Direct zero-shot prompting shows confirmation bias, with GPT-5.3 scoring pixel motion instead of task progress on one video.

sections.body: D&A replaces a single reward call with a describer D and an assessor A. The describer narrates the full trajectory without seeing the instruction, which the authors say avoids confirmation bias. An entity extractor first lists scene entities, both task-relevant and irrelevant, and the grounded describer narrates the video anchored to those entities. The assessor first writes a natural-language success criterion for the instruction, then scores each timestep of the description against that criterion, yielding dense rewards from 0 to 1. A feedback generator can also output failure analysis and corrective instructions. To reduce cost, the method downsamples T frames to H frames, with H=8 as an example, and interpolates rewards back to length T. The authors report that naive assessment collapses to all zeros or to a binary 0-to-1 interpolation.
sections.heading: D&A: Decoupling Description and Assessment
sections.headline: D&A splits reward estimation into an instruction-blind description step and a rubric-based assessment step.

sections.body: This section compares D&A with three post-trained models (RoboReward, Robometer, SOLE-R1, all on Qwen-3-VL) and zero-shot Naive VLM, GVL, and TOPReward. Gemini 3 Flash is the default base model, and GPT-6 Astra is reported as D&A*. In online RL on a DROID kitchen task, D&A raised success to 100% in ~90 minutes, while TOPReward left success at 5%. In offline RL on a bimanual YAM, D&A improved BC by +80%. In advantage-filtered behavior cloning, D&A completed the task in 18.8±1.8 seconds versus 28.5±9.2 seconds for the baseline. On D&A-Bench, D&A scored 0.67, above Robometer at 0.56 and RoboReward at 0.43, while zero-shot TOPReward and GVL scored 0.24 and 0.27.
sections.heading: Experimental Evaluation
sections.headline: D&A is competitive with post-trained reward models across three benchmarks and improves real-world policy learning.

sections.body: The limitations section states that D&A inherits constraints of frontier models, including high inference latency, token cost, and restricted context windows. These models are usually accessed through closed APIs, which adds stochasticity and limits control. They also remain prone to semantic hallucinations that can degrade description fidelity and reward assessment. Second, rewards are bounded by the granularity of natural language descriptions, which poses challenges for domains needing precise spatial relationships or absolute geometric distances. The authors conclude that D&A marks a shift from fine-tuning toward zero-shot robotics reward modeling that scales with frontier VLM advances.
sections.heading: Limitations and Discussion
sections.headline: D&A depends on closed frontier models with high latency and token cost, and it cannot express rewards that are hard to verbalize.

sections.body: The appendix gives full derivations for advantage-conditioned offline RL and for latent-space noise steering in online RL with DSRL. It adds a table comparing D&A with GPT-6 Astra against the best reported results on each benchmark, RoboRewardBenchmark MAE results, and additional VOC results. It reports gains on frontier models and the Gemini family, and average cost, wall clock time, and tokens per trajectory over 567 trajectories on RBM-EVAL-OOD. It also describes the CaP experiment setup on LIBERO, the D&A-Bench dataset of 14 real-world manipulation tasks, and the full prompts with failure analysis examples.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers RL derivations, extra benchmark tables, cost and latency, CaP details, the D&A-Bench dataset, and full prompts.
